stem: By looking at a plant externally can you tell whether a plant is \(\text{C}_3\) or \(\text{C}_4\)? Why and how?
solution:
**No.** A plant cannot be reliably identified as \(\text{C}_3\) or \(\text{C}_4\) from its external appearance.

1. **Why:** the two groups differ in their **internal leaf anatomy** (**Kranz anatomy** in \(\text{C}_4\) plants) and in their **biochemistry** (the first product of \(\text{CO}_2\) fixation is the 3-carbon **PGA** in \(\text{C}_3\) plants and the 4-carbon **OAA** in \(\text{C}_4\) plants). None of these features can be seen from outside.
2. **Only a hint from outside:** \(\text{C}_4\) plants are adapted to **dry tropical regions**, tolerate higher temperatures and respond to high light intensities, so a plant growing well in a hot, dry, sunny habitat (e.g. maize, sorghum) may be a \(\text{C}_4\) plant. This is not conclusive.
3. **How to tell for certain:** cut a **vertical section of the leaf** and observe it under the microscope. The presence of large **bundle sheath cells** around the vascular bundles (Kranz anatomy) identifies a \(\text{C}_4\) plant.
groundedIn: §11.7; §11.8 — first CO2 fixation product PGA (C3) vs OAA (C4); C4 plants adapted to dry tropical regions, tolerate higher temperatures, respond to high light; maize, sorghum; vertical leaf sections, presence of bundle sheath identifies C4 plants

stem: By looking at which internal structure of a plant can you tell whether a plant is \(\text{C}_3\) or \(\text{C}_4\)? Explain.
solution:
The **anatomy of the leaf**, seen in a **vertical section**: the presence of **Kranz anatomy** identifies a \(\text{C}_4\) plant.

1. **\(\text{C}_4\) leaf:** the vascular bundles are surrounded by particularly large **bundle sheath cells**. 'Kranz' means **'wreath'** and reflects this arrangement of cells. The bundle sheath cells may form several layers around the vascular bundles and have a **large number of chloroplasts**, **thick walls impervious to gaseous exchange** and **no intercellular spaces**. They carry out the Calvin cycle.
2. **\(\text{C}_3\) leaf:** Kranz anatomy is absent. The bundle sheath cells are not specialised in this way (they have few or no chloroplasts), and the Calvin cycle takes place in all the **mesophyll cells**.

So a section showing chloroplast-rich bundle sheath cells forming a wreath around each vascular bundle is of a \(\text{C}_4\) plant (e.g. maize, sorghum); one without them is of a \(\text{C}_3\) plant.
groundedIn: §11.8 — large bundle sheath cells around vascular bundles, Kranz means wreath, several layers, many chloroplasts, thick walls impervious to gaseous exchange, no intercellular spaces; maize, sorghum; Calvin pathway in all mesophyll cells of C3 plants and only in bundle sheath cells of C4 plants; BEYOND CHAPTER: bundle sheath cells of C3 leaves have few or no chloroplasts

stem: Even though a very few cells in a \(\text{C}_4\) plant carry out the biosynthetic – Calvin pathway, yet they are highly productive. Can you discuss why?
solution:
\(\text{C}_4\) plants are highly productive because their few Calvin-cycle cells (the **bundle sheath cells**) are supplied by a mechanism that **concentrates \(\text{CO}_2\)** at RuBisCO, so carbon fixation is very efficient.

1. **Initial fixation in the mesophyll:** \(\text{CO}_2\) is fixed by **PEP carboxylase (PEPcase)** onto PEP to form the \(\text{C}_4\) acid **OAA**, which is converted to malic or aspartic acid and transported to the bundle sheath cells.
2. **High \(\text{CO}_2\) at RuBisCO:** in the bundle sheath cells these \(\text{C}_4\) acids are broken down to release \(\text{CO}_2\), **increasing the intracellular \(\text{CO}_2\) concentration** at the enzyme site. The thick bundle sheath walls are impervious to gaseous exchange.
3. **No photorespiration:** with high \(\text{CO}_2\), RuBisCO functions as a **carboxylase** and its oxygenase activity is minimised. **Photorespiration**, which releases \(\text{CO}_2\) with the use of ATP and makes no sugar, does not occur, so fixed carbon is not lost.
4. **Well-equipped bundle sheath cells:** they have a large number of chloroplasts and are rich in RuBisCO.
5. **High light and temperature:** \(\text{C}_4\) plants respond to high light intensities and to higher temperatures with a higher rate of photosynthesis.

Hence, although fewer cells run the Calvin pathway, \(\text{C}_4\) plants show **greater productivity of biomass** and better yields.
groundedIn: §11.8; §11.9; §11.10.3 — PEPcase in mesophyll forms OAA, then malic or aspartic acid moved to bundle sheath; C4 acids broken down to release CO2; bundle sheath rich in RuBisCO, many chloroplasts, thick walls; raised intracellular CO2 makes RuBisCO act as carboxylase; C4 plants lack photorespiration so productivity and yields are better; respond to high light and higher temperatures

stem: RuBisCO is an enzyme that acts both as a carboxylase and oxygenase. Why do you think RuBisCO carries out more carboxylation in \(\text{C}_4\) plants?
solution:
Because \(\text{C}_4\) plants **raise the \(\text{CO}_2\) concentration at the site of RuBisCO**, so \(\text{CO}_2\), not \(\text{O}_2\), binds to the enzyme.

1. The active site of RuBisCO can bind both \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{O}_2\). The binding is **competitive**: the **relative concentration** of \(\text{O}_2\) and \(\text{CO}_2\) determines which of the two binds.
2. In \(\text{C}_4\) plants RuBisCO is present only in the **bundle sheath cells**; the mesophyll cells lack it.
3. The \(\text{C}_4\) acid formed in the mesophyll is broken down in the bundle sheath cells to release \(\text{CO}_2\). This **increases the intracellular \(\text{CO}_2\) concentration** around RuBisCO.
4. With \(\text{CO}_2\) at a high concentration, RuBisCO functions as a **carboxylase**: \(\text{RuBP} + \text{CO}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{RuBisCO}} 2 \times 3\text{PGA}\). Its **oxygenase** activity, which forms phosphoglycolate in photorespiration, is minimised.

In \(\text{C}_3\) plants, by contrast, some \(\text{O}_2\) does bind to RuBisCO, so \(\text{CO}_2\) fixation is decreased by photorespiration.
groundedIn: §11.9; §11.8 — active site binds both CO2 and O2, binding competitive, relative concentration decides; RuBP + CO2 gives 2 x 3PGA; C4 acid broken down in bundle sheath raises intracellular CO2 so RuBisCO functions as carboxylase minimising oxygenase activity; mesophyll lacks RuBisCO, bundle sheath rich in it; in C3 plants some O2 binds, decreasing CO2 fixation

stem: Suppose there were plants that had a high concentration of Chlorophyll b, but lacked chlorophyll a, would it carry out photosynthesis? Then why do plants have chlorophyll b and other accessory pigments?
solution:
**No.** A plant with chlorophyll b but no chlorophyll a would not carry out photosynthesis.

1. **Chlorophyll a is the chief pigment** associated with photosynthesis.
2. In each photosystem a **single chlorophyll a molecule forms the reaction centre**: **P700** in PS I and **P680** in PS II. Its electrons are excited by light and passed to the electron acceptor, which starts electron transport.
3. All the other pigments, chlorophyll b included, form the light harvesting system (**antennae**). They absorb light and **transfer the energy to chlorophyll a**. Without chlorophyll a there is no reaction centre to use this energy, so the light reaction, and with it photosynthesis, cannot take place.

**Why plants have chlorophyll b and other accessory pigments** (xanthophylls, carotenoids):

1. They absorb light of **different wavelengths**, enabling a **wider range of wavelengths** of incoming light to be utilised, which makes photosynthesis more efficient.
2. They pass the absorbed energy on to chlorophyll a.
3. They **protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation**.
groundedIn: §11.4; §11.5; §11.6; Fig. 11.4 — chlorophyll a the chief pigment; accessory pigments absorb light and transfer energy to chlorophyll a, enable a wider range of wavelengths, protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation; antennae; single chlorophyll a molecule forms the reaction centre, P700 and P680; reaction centre electrons excited and picked up by an acceptor

stem: Why is the colour of a leaf kept in the dark frequently yellow, or pale green? Which pigment do you think is more stable?
solution:
A leaf kept in the dark becomes yellow or pale green because it **loses its chlorophyll**, while its yellow pigments remain.

1. The colour of a leaf is due to four pigments: **chlorophyll a** (bright or blue green), **chlorophyll b** (yellow green), **xanthophylls** (yellow) and **carotenoids** (yellow to yellow-orange).
2. In the dark, chlorophyll is not synthesised and the chlorophyll already present breaks down.
3. The xanthophylls and carotenoids persist, so their **yellow** colour is unmasked. Where some chlorophyll is still left, the leaf looks **pale green**.

**The carotenoids and xanthophylls are more stable** than chlorophyll.
groundedIn: §11.4 — leaf colour due to four pigments: chlorophyll a (bright or blue green), chlorophyll b (yellow green), xanthophylls (yellow), carotenoids (yellow to yellow-orange); BEYOND CHAPTER: chlorophyll is not synthesised in the dark and breaks down; carotenoids and xanthophylls are more stable than chlorophyll

stem: Look at leaves of the same plant on the shady side and compare it with the leaves on the sunny side. Or, compare the potted plants kept in the sunlight with those in the shade. Which of them has leaves that are darker green ? Why?
solution:
The leaves on the **shady side** (and of the potted plants kept **in the shade**) are **darker green**.

1. Light is rarely a limiting factor in nature, **except for plants in shade** or in dense forests. A shade leaf receives low light intensity, at which the rate of photosynthesis rises directly with light; light is the **limiting factor**.
2. To trap as much of this limited light as possible, shade leaves contain **more chlorophyll**, which makes them darker green.
3. Leaves in the sun receive high light intensity. An increase in incident light beyond a point causes the **breakdown of chlorophyll**, so sun leaves carry less chlorophyll and look lighter green.
groundedIn: §11.10.1; Fig. 11.10 — light rarely limiting except for plants in shade or dense forests; linear relationship between light and CO2 fixation at low light; increase in incident light beyond a point causes breakdown of chlorophyll; BEYOND CHAPTER: shade leaves contain more chlorophyll to trap more of the limited light

context: Figure 11.10 shows the effect of light on the rate of photosynthesis. Based on the graph, answer the following questions:
stem: At which point/s (A, B or C) in the curve is light a limiting factor?
solution:
Light is a limiting factor in region **A**, and partly at **B**.

1. **A:** the rate of photosynthesis rises **linearly** with light intensity, so any change in light changes the rate directly; light is the factor nearest its minimal value.
2. **B:** the curve begins to level off; light is still partly limiting, but other factors are starting to limit the rate.
3. **C:** the rate shows no further increase with more light, so light is **not** a limiting factor there.
groundedIn: §11.10; §11.10.1; Fig. 11.10 — Blackman's law: rate determined by the factor nearest its minimal value; linear relationship between incident light and CO2 fixation at low light intensities; at higher intensities the rate does not increase further as other factors become limiting

context: Figure 11.10 shows the effect of light on the rate of photosynthesis. Based on the graph, answer the following questions:
stem: What could be the limiting factor/s in region A?
solution:
**Light (light intensity)** is the limiting factor in region A.

In region A the rate of photosynthesis increases in direct (linear) proportion to light intensity. Light is therefore the factor nearest its minimal value and, by Blackman's **Law of Limiting Factors**, it determines the rate. The other factors, such as \(\text{CO}_2\) concentration and temperature, are not yet limiting in this region.
groundedIn: §11.10; §11.10.1; Fig. 11.10 — Law of Limiting Factors; linear relationship between incident light and CO2 fixation rates at low light intensities; other factors become limiting only at higher light intensities

context: Figure 11.10 shows the effect of light on the rate of photosynthesis. Based on the graph, answer the following questions:
stem: What do C and D represent on the curve?
solution:
**C** represents the region of **light saturation**: a further increase in light intensity produces no further increase in the rate of photosynthesis, because other factors (such as \(\text{CO}_2\) concentration and temperature) have become limiting. The rate stays at its maximum value, E.

**D** represents the **light intensity at which saturation is reached**, i.e. the lowest light intensity that gives the maximum rate of photosynthesis. Light saturation occurs at about **10 per cent of full sunlight**.
groundedIn: §11.10.1; Fig. 11.10 — at higher light intensities the rate does not show further increase as other factors become limiting; light saturation occurs at 10 per cent of the full sunlight

solution:
In the \(\text{C}_3\) pathway the first product of \(\text{CO}_2\) fixation is a 3-carbon acid (**PGA**); in the \(\text{C}_4\) pathway it is a 4-carbon acid (**OAA**). Both make sugar through the Calvin cycle.

| Basis of difference | \(\text{C}_3\) pathway | \(\text{C}_4\) pathway |
|---|---|---|
| Primary \(\text{CO}_2\) acceptor | **RuBP**, a 5-carbon ketose sugar | **PEP** (phosphoenol pyruvate), a 3-carbon molecule |
| First stable product | **3-PGA** (3 carbons) | **OAA** (4 carbons) |
| Enzyme of first \(\text{CO}_2\) fixation | **RuBisCO** | **PEPcase** (PEP carboxylase) |
| Cells involved | Mesophyll cells only; Calvin cycle in all mesophyll cells | Mesophyll cells (initial fixation) and bundle sheath cells (Calvin cycle) |
| RuBisCO present in | Mesophyll cells | Bundle sheath cells only; mesophyll cells lack it |
| Leaf anatomy | No Kranz anatomy | **Kranz anatomy** |
| Photorespiration | **Present**; \(\text{CO}_2\) fixation decreased | **Absent** (negligible) |
| \(\text{CO}_2\) saturation | Only beyond 450 \(\mu\text{l L}^{-1}\); present \(\text{CO}_2\) levels are limiting | About 360 \(\mu\text{l L}^{-1}\) |
| Temperature optimum | Lower (about 20-25 \(^\circ\)C) | Higher (about 30-40 \(^\circ\)C) |
| Response to high light intensity | Lower | Respond to high light intensities |
| Productivity of biomass | Lower | Greater |
| Examples | Tomato, bell pepper | Maize, sorghum |
groundedIn: §11.7; §11.7.1; §11.7.2; §11.8; §11.9; §11.10.2; §11.10.3; Table 11.1 — PGA vs OAA; RuBP 5-carbon acceptor; PEP 3-carbon acceptor and PEPcase in mesophyll; RuBisCO in bundle sheath, mesophyll lack it; Kranz anatomy; C4 lack photorespiration; CO2 saturation 360 vs beyond 450 µl/L; C4 higher temperature optimum; tomatoes and bell pepper as CO2-responsive C3 crops; maize, sorghum; BEYOND CHAPTER: temperature optima of about 20-25 °C (C3) and 30-40 °C (C4)

solution:
Both are **photophosphorylation**, the synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate in the presence of light. They differ as follows:

| Basis of difference | Cyclic photophosphorylation | Non-cyclic photophosphorylation |
|---|---|---|
| Photosystems involved | **PS I only** | **PS II and PS I**, working in series |
| Path of electrons | The excited electron is **cycled back to the PS I complex** through the electron transport chain | Electrons pass from PS II uphill to an acceptor, down the electron transport chain to PS I, and finally to \(\text{NADP}^+\) (**Z scheme**) |
| Source of electrons | The PS I reaction centre itself (the electron returns to it) | **Water**, split in association with PS II |
| Splitting of water and release of \(\text{O}_2\) | Does not occur | Occurs |
| Products | **ATP only** | **ATP and NADPH + H\(^+\)** |
| NADP reductase | Not involved | Reduces \(\text{NADP}^+\) to NADPH + H\(^+\) |
| Likely site | **Stroma lamellae** (lack PS II and NADP reductase) | **Grana lamellae** (have both PS I and PS II) |
| When it occurs | When only PS I is functional, or when only light of wavelengths beyond 680 nm is available | When both photosystems are functional |
groundedIn: §11.6; §11.6.1; §11.6.2; §11.6.3; Fig. 11.5; Fig. 11.6 — photophosphorylation defined; non-cyclic: PS II then PS I in series, Z scheme, ATP and NADPH + H+; water splitting associated with PS II; cyclic: only PS I functional, electron cycled back to PS I, only ATP, stroma lamellae lack PS II and NADP reductase, occurs with light beyond 680 nm; NADP reductase reduces NADP+

stem: Anatomy of leaf in \(\text{C}_3\) and \(\text{C}_4\) plants
solution:
The leaf of a \(\text{C}_4\) plant shows **Kranz anatomy**; the leaf of a \(\text{C}_3\) plant does not.

| Basis of difference | Leaf of \(\text{C}_3\) plant | Leaf of \(\text{C}_4\) plant |
|---|---|---|
| Kranz anatomy | **Absent** | **Present** ('Kranz' means 'wreath', the arrangement of cells around the vascular bundles) |
| Bundle sheath cells | Not specialised; few or no chloroplasts | **Particularly large**, may form several layers around the vascular bundles, with a **large number of chloroplasts** |
| Walls and spaces of bundle sheath | Not specialised | **Thick walls impervious to gaseous exchange**; **no intercellular spaces** |
| Mesophyll cells | Carry out the Calvin cycle; contain RuBisCO | Carry out initial \(\text{CO}_2\) fixation with PEPcase; **lack RuBisCO** |
| Cell types that fix \(\text{CO}_2\) | **One**: mesophyll | **Two**: mesophyll and bundle sheath |
| Site of Calvin cycle | All the mesophyll cells | Only the bundle sheath cells |
| Examples | Tomato, bell pepper | Maize, sorghum |
groundedIn: §11.8; §11.10.2; Table 11.1 — large bundle sheath cells, Kranz means wreath, several layers, many chloroplasts, thick walls impervious to gaseous exchange, no intercellular spaces; mesophyll cells lack RuBisCO and form OAA by PEPcase; Calvin pathway in all mesophyll cells of C3 and only bundle sheath cells of C4; number of cell types fixing CO2; maize, sorghum; tomatoes and bell pepper as C3 crops; BEYOND CHAPTER: bundle sheath cells of C3 leaves are unspecialised with few or no chloroplasts
